title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 41
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: Counting Everybody
passages.text:
A. Counting a population is an act of government before it is an act of statistics, and the earliest counts make no secret of it. They were conducted to establish who could be taxed and who could be conscripted, they recorded households rather than persons, and they routinely omitted whole categories of people who were of no interest for either purpose. A count is shaped by the question it was built to answer.

B. The modern census inverted the relationship between the count and its uses. Instead of counting in order to extract, states began counting in order to allocate — seats in a legislature, funds for schools and hospitals, the placement of infrastructure — which changed the incentives of everyone involved. When a count determines what a region receives, being counted becomes valuable and being missed becomes expensive.

C. Undercounting is the technical problem that dominates the field and it is never random. The people missed are disproportionately those without stable addresses, those who move frequently, those who distrust officials and those whose households do not fit the form's assumptions, and these are the same populations whose needs the resulting allocations are supposed to address. An error that fell evenly would be a nuisance; one that falls on the same groups repeatedly is a structural bias.

D. The categories a census offers determine what can later be known. A form that asks about ethnicity, language, religion or disability in particular terms produces data in those terms and none in others, and a category that is not offered becomes statistically invisible regardless of how many people it describes. Deciding what to ask is therefore a political act performed years before any number is published.

E. Confidentiality is the condition on which the whole exercise depends and it has been broken. Census data has historically been used against the populations that supplied it, and the memory of such episodes measurably reduces participation generations later. The legal protections that now exist are strong and were built in response to specific abuses, which is the reason to take seriously the objection that they could be weakened again.

F. Administrative data is replacing the traditional count in several countries and the trade is genuine rather than obvious. Records already held — tax, health, registration, benefits — can produce population figures continuously and cheaply, without asking anyone anything; they also inherit the gaps of the systems that generated them, missing exactly the people who interact least with the state, and they answer only the questions those systems happened to record.

passages.title: Fire Belongs Here
passages.text:
Many of the world's ecosystems are shaped by fire in the way that others are shaped by rainfall, and treating fire as an external disaster in such places has produced most of the problem now attributed to it. Plants in fire-prone regions carry adaptations that only make sense in a burning landscape: bark thick enough to insulate living tissue, seeds released only by heat, buds buried where flame cannot reach, and root systems that resprout within weeks of a fire that removed everything above ground.

The pattern matters more than the presence. Frequent low-intensity fire consumes the litter and small growth on the ground while leaving mature trees alive, and an ecosystem adapted to that pattern is not adapted to a rare, extremely hot fire that kills everything, or to no fire at all. Two landscapes can burn the same total area over a century and be entirely different places depending on how that burning was distributed.

Suppressing every fire produces the fire nobody can suppress. Fuel that would have burned in small quantities repeatedly instead accumulates for decades, and when ignition eventually occurs under bad conditions the resulting fire is hotter, larger and beyond the reach of any response — a fire whose severity is a product of the previous policy rather than of the weather alone. The effect is well documented and took a long time to be accepted because each individual suppression decision was locally correct.

Deliberate burning under controlled conditions is the principal remedy and the hardest thing to do at scale. The conditions in which a fire can be lit safely are a narrow band of humidity, wind and fuel moisture that occurs on relatively few days; the smoke is unpopular and has real health effects; and any escape becomes a career-ending event for whoever authorised it. The asymmetry of consequences — no reward for fires prevented, severe blame for one that escapes — reliably produces too little burning.

Where people live has changed faster than any of this. Housing built into vegetated landscapes places structures where fire is a normal process, and the resulting losses are commonly reported as a fire problem when they are substantially a building and planning problem. What determines whether a house survives is largely its construction, its roof, its vents and the treatment of the few metres immediately around it, and those are decisions made long before any fire starts.

The climate contribution is real and is frequently used to obscure the rest. Longer dry seasons and more extreme fire weather increase the area burned and the difficulty of control, and they act on landscapes already loaded with fuel and populated at their edges. Treating the whole problem as climate change removes attention from the two things that can be changed within a season: what is built, and what is burned deliberately.

passages.title: Paying to Be Noticed
passages.text:
Advertising is defended as information and criticised as manipulation, and the more useful description is neither. Most advertising conveys little information and persuades few people directly; what it does reliably is establish which products a person can bring to mind, and being thought of at the moment of choosing is worth a great deal in categories where the options are otherwise similar. The function is memory rather than argument.

Much of the spending is defensive, which explains why total expenditure stays high while individual campaigns show poor returns. If competitors advertise and one firm stops, it loses share; if all stop, all would be better off; nobody can stop unilaterally. The result is an arms race whose costs are eventually paid by consumers in prices, and which produces very little that anyone would miss if it vanished simultaneously.

Measurement is where the industry's difficulties concentrate. The people who see an advertisement for a product are disproportionately people already inclined to buy it, so naive measurement credits the advertisement with sales that would have occurred anyway; properly controlled experiments, where some potential customers are randomly withheld from seeing the campaign, repeatedly find effects far smaller than the reported figures. The methods that produce flattering numbers remain in wide use for the obvious reason.

Targeting was expected to resolve this and has partly compounded it. Showing advertisements to people most likely to buy improves the measured return precisely because those people were most likely to buy regardless, so the better the targeting, the more the measurement overstates the effect. The industry has built an apparatus of extraordinary technical sophistication on a metric that becomes less trustworthy as the apparatus improves.

The intermediary layer takes a share that nobody chose. Between an advertiser's payment and a publisher's receipt sit exchanges, verification services, data brokers and agencies, and studies attempting to trace money through this chain have repeatedly failed to account for a substantial fraction of it — not through fraud in most cases, but through complexity that no participant has an interest in reducing.

What advertising unambiguously does is fund things that would otherwise be paid for directly. Search, social platforms, most journalism and much broadcasting exist in their present form because attention can be sold, and the alternative is not the same services without advertisements but different services with subscriptions and a different set of people excluded. The choice is between funding models with different distributions of cost, and the pretence that one is simply free is what makes the argument confused.
